title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the missing quality, the nearest subject, and the sentence that names the catastrophe

questions.prompt: A pupil must complete this paragraph with its opening sentence. "……… Growth must be checked to avoid this catastrophe. Many environmental, social and economic problems are either caused or increased by overpopulation." Which sentence belongs in the gap?

options.text: Many countries have already introduced their own family-planning programmes.
The world's population will soon outgrow the resources that sustain it.
Overpopulation is a problem that worries a great many people today.
Growth is the engine of every economy and must be encouraged.

questions.explanation: The second sentence says this catastrophe, and this must point back to something already named — so the opening sentence has to describe a catastrophe, which is what running out of resources does. Family-planning programmes are a response rather than a disaster, and nothing in the paragraph refers back to them. Saying that overpopulation worries people names a worry, not the catastrophe itself, so this would still have nothing to attach to. And praising growth contradicts the very next sentence, which says growth must be checked.

questions.prompt: Two brothers, Peter and John, are both keen on pop music. Which sentence reports that with not only … but also?

options.text: Not only Peter but also John is a pop fan.
Not only Peter and John are pop fans.
Not only Peter but also John are pop fans.
Peter is not only a pop fan but also John.

questions.explanation: With two subjects joined by this structure, the verb agrees with the nearer one, and the nearer one is John — singular, so the verb is is and the noun that follows becomes singular too. Keeping are copies the agreement of the original sentence, where both Peter and John made a plural subject, and that is precisely the trap. Replacing but also by and leaves not only stranded without its partner. And the last version joins a pop fan to John, which are not the same kind of element and produce a sentence that says Peter is John.

questions.prompt: Turn these into one sentence: "The grass is very wet. We can't sit on it." and "The case is very light. I can carry it." Which pair of transformations is right?

options.text: The grass is wet enough to sit on. / The case is too light to carry.
The grass is too wet to sit on. / The case is light enough to carry.
The grass is too wet to sit on it. / The case is light enough to carry it.
The grass is not dry enough to sit on. / The case is too light to carry it.
The grass is wet enough to sit on it. / The case is not heavy enough to carry.

questions.explanation: Ask each time whether the action happens. Sitting does not, because of an excess of wetness, so the grass takes too wet to sit on; carrying does happen, because the lightness suffices, so the case takes light enough to carry. Swapping the two structures reverses both meanings at once. Adding it after the verb doubles the object, since the grass and the case are already the subjects. Changing wet into dry is a legitimate rewriting but is not what the exercise asks, and it is paired here with a wrong second half. And calling the case not heavy enough turns a success into a failure.

questions.prompt: Your book prints on page 148 that "global warming is a fact today", and on page 151 that "scientists are uncertain about the long-term impact on the planet's climate". Both come from 1995. How should a careful pupil use them?

options.text: Quote the second, since it is the later page.
Quote neither, since the lesson cannot be trusted at all.
Quote the mechanism and date every figure.
Quote the first and ignore the date, since it is a fact.

questions.explanation: What the lesson describes reliably is a mechanism — greenhouse gases accumulate because millions of tonnes of carbon are released each year — and mechanisms do not expire, while the measurements and the state of scientific opinion around them do, which is why every figure needs its year. Preferring the later page treats page order as chronology, and both sentences date from the same 1995 source. Rejecting the whole lesson throws away definitions and vocabulary that remain perfectly good. And keeping the first while dropping the date is exactly what makes a dated claim look current.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes: "They broke into his office, stole his books and tore up his manuscripts." and is asked to rewrite it with not only … but also. What is the difficulty?

options.text: The three verbs are in the wrong tense to carry the structure properly.
The sentence has no subject to attach the structure to.
The structure cannot be used with verbs at all.
The structure has two slots and the sentence has three actions.

questions.explanation: not only and but also mark exactly two elements, so three actions do not fit without grouping two of them together — for instance not only broke into his office but also stole his books and tore up his manuscripts. The tense is not the obstacle: the structure works in any tense, provided the two elements match. Nor is it barred from verbs, since they not only smoke but also drink is one of the book's own examples. And the sentence has a perfectly clear subject in they, which is what would carry the structure once the actions are grouped.

questions.prompt: Which sentence places its adverb of degree correctly?

options.text: There is not enough time to purify all the waste water.
There is not time enough of purifying all the waste water.
There is not too time to purify all the waste water.
There is not quite time enough purify all the waste water.

questions.explanation: Here enough governs a noun rather than an adjective, and before a noun it comes first: enough time. That is the half of the rule pupils forget, because with an adjective the word goes after — warm enough, thick enough. Placing it after the noun and then replacing to by of breaks the structure twice over, since enough to keeps its to. too cannot introduce a noun in this way at all. And the last version drops the to that must stand before purify, leaving two verbs side by side with nothing to join them.
